clue.text: Swimmer fine as filth swirls around

indicators.note: whatever swirls around is churned up and resettles in a different order

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade and abbreviation for fine
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fish sits in murky water while dirt swirls around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' is not an adjective here but the single letter F, which joins AS and FILTH to make eight letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A flounder, plaice or sole is a bottom-dwelling fish, so it is one kind of swimmer.

clue.text: Wiggling of toe is flirtatious activity

indicators.note: something wiggling moves about, so the letters shift out of their printed order

parts.note: three words taken letter for letter as the material to rearrange

explanation.surface: Wiggling one's toe under the table is a flirtatious move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' and 'is' look like grammar words, but they supply letters along with 'toe'; the surface even describes what the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing footsie means secretly touching someone's feet under a table as a flirting game.

definitions.note: Wow is used here as a verb, to impress greatly

parts.note: A is the top grade in exams
a maze is a puzzle of paths

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at an excellent puzzle and exclaims in delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wow!' reads like an exclamation tacked on, but it is the definition, taken as the verb meaning to astonish.
explanation.definitionFit: To wow an audience is to astonish or greatly impress them, a direct synonym.

parts.note: to overlook something is to fail to remember it
the writer of the clue refers to themself as me
the negative, moved to the end as the phrase is reworded

explanation.surface: A writer pleads not to be passed over, then admits a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't overlook the writer' is reworded into an old-fashioned plea, with the negative moving to the end. 'Bloomer' looks like a mistake but is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Forget-me-not is a small blue flowering plant, and anything that blooms can be called a bloomer in crosswords.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one part wraps round another
in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
camp means theatrically affected or exaggerated in manner

explanation.surface: Someone is distressed about seafood that has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' looks like part of the story about spoiled food, but it means mannered or showy, which is CAMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are langoustines or large prawns, usually served fried in breadcrumbs, a seafood dish.

clue.text: Period celebrated by mother and son

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as by, as in three by four
Ma is an informal word for mother
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A season that a mother and her son mark together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' seems to link the period to the people celebrating it, but it supplies the letter X, the times sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas is a festive season, a stretch of the calendar marked with festivities.

clue.text: Fail to notice one on purpose

parts.note: to miss something is to fail to notice it
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone deliberately fails to see a person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On purpose' reads as one idiom meaning deliberately; split it, and 'on' is wordplay while 'purpose' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mission is a calling or goal someone pursues, so it is a sense of purpose or aim.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
XI, eleven, is a cricket or football side

explanation.surface: A reserve side brings fresh vigour to the game.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'second XI' is a reserve team, but here 'second' gives S and XI, the number eleven, is a team of that many players.
explanation.definitionFit: To have steam or run out of steam is idiomatic for having or lacking power and vigour.

clue.text: No backing with tune being broadcast

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
an air is a tune or melody

explanation.surface: A song goes out on radio without any backing band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No backing' suggests an unaccompanied performance, but 'backing' tells you to reverse the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme that is on air is currently being transmitted on radio or television.

indicators.note: in tells you the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A performer playing in the Tasmanian city of Hobart is awful.
explanation.walkthrough: Hobart is the capital of Tasmania; the city name only supplies its last four letters to the run.
explanation.definitionFit: An artiste is a professional performer such as a singer or dancer, so it is an entertainer.

clue.text: Article on fielder in Carol Reed film

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the first part comes first

parts.note: the definite article
third man is a fielding position in cricket, near the boundary behind the slips

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about a cricket player who appears in a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket names fielders by their positions, and third man is one of them, so the player is the position.
explanation.definitionFit: The Third Man is the 1949 noir thriller directed by Carol Reed, set in postwar Vienna.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to look at or notice
second meaning: the diocese or throne of a bishop

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as an order to look at a bishop's chair; it is two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to watch or perceive, while the noun names the district or throne from which a bishop governs.

parts.note: surface reading: someone has walked out on us and gone
setter's reading: the phrase 'left us' is a gentle way of saying 'dead', so the answer is a term for such polite substitutes

explanation.surface: Someone has abandoned us, leaving us for dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left for dead' is the idiom you hear first; instead read 'left us' as a softened stand-in for 'dead', and ask what such a phrase is called.
explanation.definitionFit: A softened, indirect expression used in place of a blunt or painful word is called this.

indicators.note: in places one part inside another
complex means intricate and tangled, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written; anime is Japanese animation
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A puzzle appears inside a complicated Japanese cartoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' reads as describing the anime's plot, but it signals rearranging its letters before G goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a mystery or puzzling thing, a close synonym for riddle.

clue.text: Uranium in engine bad for naive female

indicators.note: in places one part inside another
bad means broken or faulty, so the word is put together wrongly

parts.note: taken as written
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Nuclear fuel in a faulty engine spells trouble for an innocent young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' seems to describe the engine, but it signals that ENGINE's letters are rearranged around the uranium symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingenue is an innocent, unsophisticated young woman, especially as a stock role in plays.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to switch, as when moving between trains
second meaning: coins, or the cash returned after paying

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to move funds; the two parts are separate meanings, one verb and one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To transfer between buses or trains is to switch over, and loose coins in your pocket are called this too.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Samuel Beckett's play from the Theatre of the Absurd
second meaning: the closing phase of a chess game or contest

explanation.surface: A ridiculous scene breaks out during a tight game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close match' suggests a tight contest, but 'close' means the end, so it is the final stage of a match.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's one-act absurdist play bears this title, and chess players use it for the final phase of play.

indicators.note: in a down clue, one part under another is placed below it, so it comes second

parts.note: the ash is a tree
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A sheep grazes beneath a tree at a hermit's retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: Because this is a down clue, the piece 'under' the tree is written below it, so the tree comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashram is a secluded religious retreat in India, a community place of withdrawal much like a hermitage.

indicators.note: possibly means in one of the ways things could be, so try another arrangement of the letters

parts.note: three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a person is a manager or perhaps a singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a conjunction offering alternatives, but it is part of the letters to rearrange. The British spelling uses S rather than Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who arranges events and coordinates people is in charge of them, much as a manager is.

parts.note: O is round in shape
O looks like the digit zero
mph, miles per hour, is a measure of speed

explanation.surface: A driver circles a track while barely moving at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like a verb about motoring, but it is a noun meaning energy; 'round' and 'zero' each give an O.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is vigour, energy or enthusiasm, the same sense as drive meaning ambition or push.

clue.text: Small boy wanting first to lie down

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word it qualifies

parts.note: the opening letter of the second word, which is removed

explanation.surface: A little boy who would like to be the first to lie down for a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie down' reads as one phrase, but 'down' is the definition and 'first to lie' is just the letter L to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down is an idiom for being unhappy or low in spirits, which is what this adjective means.

clue.text: Rook in exotic bush, hibiscus maybe

indicators.note: in places one part inside another
exotic means foreign and unusual, so the letters take on an unfamiliar arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: A rook bird perches in a tropical bush, perhaps a hibiscus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' reads as the bird, but it is the chess piece, abbreviated R. 'Maybe' marks hibiscus as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibiscus is a flowering woody plant, one example of a low, many-stemmed bush.

indicators.note: dismissed means sent away, so a letter leaves the word

parts.note: a minister is a member of the clergy
one is I, the Roman numeral; the cleric's word has two, and the later one goes

explanation.surface: A cathedral clergyman's deputy is sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a deputy, but it picks out which of the two I's in the cleric's title is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A minster is a large or important church, as in York Minster, often with cathedral status.

clue.text: Mass with song for a von Trapp?

parts.note: M is the symbol for mass in physics
an aria is a solo song in opera

explanation.surface: A church service with singing, fitting for the musical von Trapp family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' suggests church, given the nun in the story, but it is just M. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria von Trapp was the governess turned stepmother whose family inspired The Sound of Music.

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
Ed is short for editor, the boss of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A man looks after his editor at the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attend to' reads like caring for the boss, but it is the definition meaning to listen to.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend to advice is to pay attention to it and act on it.

clue.text: Willing in the morning to empower

parts.note: a.m. marks times before noon
to enable someone is to give them the power to act

explanation.surface: Someone is ready first thing to give others authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willing' sounds like the start of a sentence about desire, but it is the definition, and the rest splits into a time label and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An amenable person is open and agreeable to suggestions, ready to go along with them.
